decidedValue.sourceUseRationale: Susie/John passages (lines 1607, 1621) reference classroom-management discourse external to lesson purpose. Adapted passages demonstrate identical structural transformation (passive → active) without unrelated topic-load.

interior1.passage: Procrastination is a problem for many students. Research has shown that it affects academic performance. Steel (2007) found that around 80–95% of students engage in procrastination. Kim and Seo (2015) looked at the relationship between procrastination and academic achievement. They found a negative correlation. Sirois (2014) examined how self-compassion affects the stress that procrastination creates. Students who procrastinate experience higher levels of stress. Tice and Baumeister (1997) suggested that procrastination provides short-term mood benefits. Students delay tasks to avoid negative emotions. Steel (2007) identified lack of self-regulation as a factor. Time management is also important according to several researchers (Häfner et al., 2014). Students need to understand why they procrastinate and develop strategies to address it.
interior1.commentary: This passage reports sources one after another but makes no argument. Each sentence describes what a researcher found, then moves on. Missing: no discourse markers signalling how sources relate; no authorial voice; no synthesis. The writing is not wrong, but it lacks a critical edge.

interior2.passage: Research has consistently demonstrated that procrastination is a widespread challenge among university students, with studies suggesting that 80–95% engage in it at some point (Steel, 2007). However, recent work has moved beyond simply documenting its prevalence to examining why students procrastinate and what can be done about it. For example, while early research framed procrastination as a time-management problem (Häfner et al., 2014), more recent studies have emphasised its emotional dimensions: students often delay tasks not because they lack planning skills but because they seek to avoid negative feelings associated with the work (Sirois, 2014). Furthermore, this emotional avoidance may provide short-term mood benefits (Tice & Baumeister, 1997), which helps explain why procrastination persists despite its costs to academic achievement (Kim & Seo, 2015). This shift in understanding has therefore led researchers to advocate for emotion-regulation strategies rather than time-management interventions alone.
interior2.commentary: Same sources, same evidence — but the writer makes a point. Transformation: argument leads (sources support); discourse markers present (however, for example, while, furthermore, therefore); synthesis into a narrative (early view → recent shift → implication). These markers are the language of criticality.

stimulus.passage: Online learning has become more common in higher education. Many universities now offer online courses. Allen and Seaman (2017) found that over 30% of students take at least one online course. Means et al. (2013) compared online and face-to-face instruction. They found that online learning can be as effective as traditional instruction. Garrison (2011) developed a framework for online learning communities. Student engagement is important. Dixson (2015) studied how students engage with online courses. Some students prefer online learning because of flexibility. Other students find it isolating. Universities need to consider how to support online learners effectively.
stimulus.instruction: Revise this passage so that it has a critical edge. Your revision should: lead with your argument, not with sources; use discourse markers (such as however, furthermore, therefore) to signal relationships between ideas; synthesise the sources into a point, rather than listing them.

feedback.content: Compare your revision to the original. A passage with a critical edge typically: opens with an authorial claim that the sources will support; uses 'however' or 'although' to signal where views differ; uses 'furthermore' or 'in addition' to build the argument; ends with a judgement ('therefore', 'this suggests that'). There is no single right answer — but the transformation should be visible.

wOpen.learningOutcomes: By the end of this course, you will be able to: recognise that different disciplines shape academic writing in distinct ways; identify how style, evidence, vocabulary, and discourse engagement vary across discipline families; evaluate and justify your own discipline's conventions; and develop a critical edge by using the language of criticality to engage actively with sources.
wOpen.overviewAndJustification: This course assumes you already know how to structure a piece of academic writing and integrate sources. Now the question shifts: what does good writing look like in *your* discipline - and how do you develop the critical voice that distinguishes competent work from excellent? You will explore how conventions vary across discipline families and learn to read your own discipline's expectations with sharper awareness.
wOpen.signpostIntro: This course moves through four lessons, each building on the last - from recognising that disciplines differ, through analysing those differences, to applying that awareness to your own field and developing a critical edge.
wOpen.signpostOutro: Each lesson pairs teaching with a quick check or reflective task, so you can test your understanding and connect the ideas to your own writing.

wClose.courseSummary: You have completed Academic Writing: Advanced Stage - four lessons on disciplinary self-awareness and critical engagement with sources.
wClose.practiceConnection: These ideas apply directly to your next piece of writing. Before you submit, ask: does my writing show awareness of my discipline's conventions? Does my critical voice come through - or am I merely reporting what others have said?
wClose.whereThisGoesNext: This is the final stage of the Academic Writing pathway. What you have learned here - reading for convention, developing a critical edge - will serve you across every writing task your degree requires.
